based on DIS and Teletesting are in particular under
development to support incoming engineering and
operational requirements, as especially addressed to
the ground engineering support for the In-Orbit
Infrastructures. The performed experiments and
on-going developments include the use of Virtual
Reality models in complex Human-ln-The-Loop,
Hardware-in-The-Loop, and Computational
Intensive simulation scenarios. The defined
Architectures are discussed together with their
utilization in the space and ground segment
frameworks.

Title: H2-H2A Redesign for More efficient and Active Space Development - Enhanced Capability and Reduced Launch Cost -
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract:
This paper presents the concept and design philosophy of the H-IIA family of launch vehicles.
The H-IIA launch vehicle improvement program has two objectives to meet diversifying launch demands in the beginning of the next century. These objectives are to enhance launch capability and versatility, and to reduce launch cost.
The H-IIA family will have two members (a standard vehicle and an augmented vehicle) by the beginning of the new century, and a larger member could join later when needed. All members have the common core vehicle that is a redesigned H-II rocket. The common core vehicle is augmented by one or two liquid rocket booster(s), which is essentially the same as the first stage of the core vehicle. Each vehicle can be a single staged or a two- staged launcher depending on mission requirements. The core stage of the standard vehicle can accommodate up to two sets of small-solid-rocket- boosters to meet slight increases of payload capability. The key of this concept is that without costly development of new propulsion systems the H-IIA family can cover a broad range of missions, 4-7.5 tons into GTO or 10-18 tons into LEO. The envisioned missions of the H-IIA family are re-supply missions to ISS/JEM, lunar and planetary missions, the flight testing of an experimental HOPE, and others in addition to launching satellites into LEO, MEO, and GTO.
In order to reduce launch costs and to achieve efficient operability, all vehicle subsystems are simplified, refined, or redesigned based on the experiences and expertise enhanced through the development and operations of the H-II rockets. The design changes are taking place in two steps: the H-IIA project and its precursor project. In the precursor project, the new fairing and the new second stage will be developed and applied to the H-II rocket launched in 1999. In the H-IIA project, the rest of the vehicle will be renewed. Following the completion of its design study phase conducted in 1995, the H-IIA project has entered the full-scale development phase in April 1996. The detailed design of the vehicle has almost completed and ground testing of major subsystems is in the final phase now. The production of the test flight vehicle, which is scheduled for launch in January or February of 2000, has started.

Title: Large Space Antenna Structural Design Technology Status
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract: The optimum design methodology for construction of future large space antenna reflectors measuring several tens of meters was developed. The goal of designing lighter larger and stiffer structures required the development of an integrated design environment in which several design criteria can simultaneously be optimized structural design parameters and weight. Developed analysis tools are used to analyze the non-linear structural response and flexible body dynamics. By using the antenna design system included the analysis tools, a modular mesh deployable antenna was developed for the future advanced mobile communication system. Present design considerations indicate that a total weight under 135 kg and an eigen frequency of more than 0.8 Hz can be achieved for the 18 x 16 m antenna reflector.

Title: Overview and Status of a Mirror Fusion Propulsion System Design Study
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract:
The main goal of this paper is to describe and emphasize the important discoveries made since 1986 in the engineering design of space fusion propulsion plants.
Among the important discoveries are four fundamental design principles (DPs) which should be used when adapting candidate Earth-based fusion- electric power plants to propulsion in space.
DPI. Maximize direct access to space for waste radiation.
DP2. Operate components as passive radiators whenever possible.
DP3. Optimize the plasma characteristics for best specific jet power
DP4. Optimize mission capability versus lifetime-mass-to-orbit (LMTO).
Another discovery is a design philosophy called IDEAs (Integrated Design Environment Algorithms) which is a tool for discovering new fundamental design principles.
These discoveries allowed us to adapt, and then to optimize, an earth-based fusion-electric magnetic-mirror-fusion reactor concept for propulsion in space. The resulting design is called the Mirror Fusion Propulsion System (MFPS); and its design status is reviewed.
This work can be used as a general road map for others attempting to convert earth-based designs to propulsion in space. It also has applicability to matter- antimatter propulsion systems engineering

Title: The ECSS Approach to Space Engineering Standardisation
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract:
The ECSS (European Cooperation for Space Standardisation) Standard System, proposed in 1993 and developed starting in 1994, today consists of about 25 published standards and about 20 draft ones covering all hight level Management, Product Assurance and Engineering definitions and requirements. Other documents are being prepared on detailed topics within each of these disciplines.
Management and Product Assurance in the space industry have been the subject of previous standardisation at company, national agency and European level. Whilst standardisation within space Engineering has been implemented at a detailed design level, there has been little previous attampt to provide a unified and comprehensive structure, valid as a common reference for the people involved on the project who are used to different cultures and markets.
The paper describes how the subject is developed and presented in two key ECSS Engineering standards:
• ECSS-E-OO, “Space Engineering: Policy and Principles”.
The typical components of the system engineering mechanism are described, illustrating how iteration and nesting of this mechanism’s operation at various deconstruction levels and at various project stages constitutes the system engineering process.
• ECSS-E-10, “ Space Engineering, System Engineering”.

Title: The Road from the NASA Access-to-Space Study to a Reusable Launch Vehicle
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract:
NASA has established a goal of providing low-cost
reliable access to space. While this goal has been around
for many years, it received a major impetus when the
U.S Congress mandated the Access-to-Space study in
1993. This study concluded that a rocket powered single-
stage-to-orbit vehicle offered the best opportunity for
low-cost reliable space transportation by the first decade
of the new millennium. This required a focused technology
development program before such a vehicle could
be built. NASA recognized that no commercial entity
would commit to the development of a single-stage-toorbit
vehicle without the U.S. Government’s participation.
To this end, NASA entered into a cooperative
agreement with industry to mature the required technologies.
This effort includes the development of an experimental
subscale-vehicle known as the X-33, an extensive
ground-based program to provide the required additional
technology development, and conceptual through preliminary
design of an operational reusable launch vehicle.
Following this effort, a decision will be made whether or
not to proceed with the detailed design and fabrication
of an operational vehicle.

Title: The Space Techology Research Vehicles (STRV) 1 c&d - Preparing for Launch
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract: The launch of the UK Defence Evaluation & Research Agency’s (DERA’s) STRV Ic&d microsatellites in the second half of 1999 is on track following the signature of a launch contract with Arianespace on 27 February 1998. The two spacecraft will be the first to use the Ariane Structure for Auxiliary Payloads (ASAP) on Ariane 5 and will be launched into a geo-synchronous transfer orbit (GTO). Between them the satellites are carrying 25 payload experiments from government, industry and academia from the UK, the US, Canada and continental Europe. The project has completed project definition and detailed design. Construction of the payload, spacecraft and its sub-assemblies is underway and assembly, integration and test (AIT) started in August this year. The paper reviews the progress to date and the work in hand in preparation for launch. It considers the challenges of managing a multi-national, multi-payload mission on a limited budget to an ambitious schedule. The management structure, methods and tools used are described, together with the technical strategy and design and modelling techniques which have been employed. An initial assessment is made of the effectiveness of these methods, some of the difficulties encountered and the lessons learned. Finally, the paper looks ahead to how these lessons will be applied in future missions.

Title: The Use of System Models in the EuroMoon Spacecraft Design
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract:
EuroMoon 2000 is a proposal to land a
spacecraft close to the south pole of the Moon,
on a “peak of eternal light", in the year 2001.
This ambitious objective, coupled with a short
timescale, necessitated the use of new methods
for system analysis and modelling. “System
Model techniques” have been developed at
MMS, creating linked component models of the
parts of the system which can be used to
predict overall performance. The System
Model is used as a design management tool to
achieve a feasible design and to carry out
trade offs of options at system level. The
“Model” starts off with simple descriptions of
component subsystems, but evolves alongside
the understanding of the system. It provides a
data base on the knowledge and design
decisions at any time, and is available
electronically to all members of the design
team, although formally controlled by the
System Architect. The approach provides
“concurrent engineering without co-located
teams” - a very necessary requirement in a
culture of multi-national teams and distributed
skill centres.

Title: Development of a 15m class modular mesh deployable antenna
Publication: IAC 1997 congress proceedings, 48th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  6–10 October 1997, Turin, Italy
Abstract: We propose a modular concept and a cable-mesh deployable antenna structure as means to constructa 15m class antenna reflector. The level of our technology has advanced to a new stage. This involves optimizing the design given the system requirements, and then fabricating engineering models and verifying their performance. An integrated design environment has been constructed to facilitate the design of extremely large but very light antenna structure. Several design criteria can be optimized simultaneously by using newly developed design and analysis tools. A newly developed analysis tool, SPADE, can analyzenon-linearstructural responses, flexible body dynamics, and thermal deformation. In addition, SPADE can aid in the design of truss members, cables, and mesh elements. Design inputs are the size of each module, properties of structural members, and truss topology. They are optimized against the total weight, eigen frequencies, thermal deformation and stowed size. Under present design considerations, we conclude that a total weight of less than 132 kg and eigen frequencies of more than 0.8 Hz can be achieved for an 18m x 16m antenna reflector. The reflector consists of 14 modules, each 4.8m in diameter. Three of the 14 modules were fabricated as engineering models which were able to verify the design method and analytically obtain the reflector’s structural/mechanical characteristics.

Title: Maintainable Design for Columbus Payloads
Publication: IAC 1997 congress proceedings, 48th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  6–10 October 1997, Turin, Italy
Abstract:
The European Space Agency is developing microgravity research facilities to outfit its Columbus module for the International Space Station. Such facilities could be operated on-orbit for several years. In the past, microgravity payload developers were dealing with short duration missions and the design was driven by safety and performances considerations. While safety remains a top priority for the International Space Station payloads, reliability and maintainability are now included among the key performances to be considered for facility type of payloads. Due to the large weight and volume of a facility, a non-recoverable (on- oibit) failure would disrupt the planned science program and entail high recovery costs for transportation to ground. A maintainable design and careful consideration of components reliability are essential elements to minimize life-cycle costs and meet the severe logistical constraints in particular crew time and upmass. This paper describes the ESA maintainability approach for Columbus facilities and provides examples of its implementation at system and detailed design level.
The paper includes a discussion of limit and values of some maintainability evaluation techniques, usually applied to more complex systems, to provide inputs for maintenance planning and spares policy.

Title: System Design and Program Status of the H-IIA Rockets
Publication: IAC 1997 congress proceedings, 48th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  6–10 October 1997, Turin, Italy
Abstract:
This paper presents the concept and design philosophy of the H-IIA rocket family, the status of development activities, and missions to be conducted in the first half of the next decade. The growth potential of the family toward the future will be presented as well.
The family will have two members by the first year of the new century, and the largest member would join later. All members have the common core vehicle that is a redesigned H-II rocket. The common core vehicle is augmented by one or two liquid rocket boosters), which is essentially equivalent to the first stage of the core vehicle. Each vehicle can be a single stage or a two-stage launcher depending on mission requirements. The key of this concept is that without developing a new propulsion system the H-IIA family will cover a broad range of missions, 4- 8 tons into GTO or 10-20 tons into LEO.
The purposes of this program are to reinforce launching capability and mission flexibility, and to reduce launching cost for more efficient and active use of space in the 21st century. The envisioned missions of the H-IIA family are the flight testing of experimental HOPE (HOPE-X, an unmanned winged return vehicle), cargo supply missions to ISS/JEM, lunar and planetary missions, and others in addition to launching satellites.
Following the completion of its design study phase conducted in 1995, the H-IIA program has entered the full-scale development phase in April 1996. The detailed design of the vehicle and ground testing of major subsystems are under way now, and the production of a test flight vehicle will be initiated at the end of this year. The first flight is scheduled for the winter of 2000.
Future plans of the H-IIA family are in a study phase now. Among many ideas, the most realistic ones are an enhancement of the second stage capability for a direct insertion into GEO and the heavy lift capability up to 4 tons into GEO or 20 tons into LEO.

Title: Integrated Thermal-Structural-Electromagnetic Design and Analysis of Spacecraft Antenna Reflectors
Publication: IAC 1996 congress proceedings, 47th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–11 October 1996, Beijing, China
Abstract:
Design and analysis of spacecraft antenna reflectors is a technically challenging task requiring consideration on many functional disciplines and associated interdisciplinary coupling. The accurate prediction of RF performance deterioration caused by thermal distortion of an antenna system require a series of sophisticated and time-consuming thermal, structural and RF performance analysis techniques. In addition, today the need to reduce design time, cost, and structure weight while improve product performance and reliability has become more and more important in the design of spacecraft. Therefore, it is essential to employ the integrated design and analysis technique and optimization method in the design of spacecraft antenna reflectors. This paper discusses interdisciplinary design and analysis techniques and optimization methodology of antenna reflectors. An implementation scheme of an integrated optimization-based design and analysis system of spacecraft antenna reflectors is described. This system is based on the CAD and CAE software widely used in CAST. It incorporates antenna reflectors structures geometry modeling, finite element modeling, thermal analysis, structural analysis, RF performance analysis and optimization techniques in an integrated environment. In this system, to eliminate modeling disparities between different disciplines and save engineering time, the same finite element model and same finite element analysis software(MSC/NASTRAN) are used in thermal analysis, structural analysis and optimization.

The design of spacecraft antenna reflector is a complex multidisciplinary design problem. In order to efficiently design light-weight reflector structure without violating multiple stringent design constraints and comply with the antenna performance requirements, this paper discusses interdisciplinary design and analysis techniques and optimization methodology of antenna reflectors, describes an implementation scheme of an integrated optimization-based design and analysis system of spacecraft antenna reflectors. Through incorporating antenna reflectors structures geometry modeling, finite element modeling, thermal analysis, structural analysis, RF performance analysis and optimization techniques in an integrated environment, this system can
provide a rigorous, efficient approach to achieve optimum reflector design giving high performance and lower mass, evaluate numerous design tradeoffs and perform antenna in-orbit performance analysis.

Title: Test Strategies for Faster, Better and Cheaper Space Systems
Publication: IAC 1996 congress proceedings, 47th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–11 October 1996, Beijing, China
Abstract: Reexamination of product assurance and testing approaches is necessary in these times of decreased space hardware resources for development. A systematic evaluation of these processes and their value-added is required. This paper describes efforts underway within the Jet Propulsion Laboratory and across NASA to reduce the cost of success of “better, faster and cheaper” missions. Approaches for risk management, and the identification and quantification of value-added processes are discussed. These approaches naturally lead to the development of systematic methods for testing and qualifying advanced technologies. To be effective, product assurance and testing processes must be implemented via concurrent engineering with an early involvement of assurance engineers. This results in a new integrated and disciplined approach to design, development and validation. This paper discusses the nature of the development process and describes the techniques in use and under development.

Title: The Analysis on Aerospace Plane Concept Studies
Publication: IAC 1996 congress proceedings, 47th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–11 October 1996, Beijing, China
Abstract:
Aerospace plane concepts studies are analyzed based on the concept comparison of space transporation system. Concept comparison is suggested for finding the optimal launch vehicle scheme. Concept comparison is composed of the concept producing and improving method and the global optimization design method.
Concept producing and improving method includes specialist knowledge base , combination of technology units, the method of analyzing and improving concept, and so on. Specialist knowledge base includes some technology factors which are sentive to design optimal space plane concept. Those factors are: Staging of TSTO launch vehicles, rendezvous of two launch vehicles; Launch and landing modes, rapid accelerating or slow accelerating ascent trajectories, climbing / orbit transfer; Liquid air cycle engine (LACE) and Rocket based combined Cycle (RBCC) technology . The factors also include some systematically engineering integrated design technology-
Global numerical optimization is composed of dynamic and static algorithm of design parameters of vehicle subsystems and/or components.
Based on five technology units, a great deal of aerospace plane concepts are produced. More than thirty kinds of aerospace plance concepts are simulated and analyzed. Some execellent concepts of minimum take-off weight are obtained.

Title: ANALYSIS AND DESIGN OF AN HEXAPOD MECHANISM FOR AUTONOMOUS PAYLOAD POINTING
Publication: IAC 1995 congress proceedings, 46th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  2–6 October 1995, Oslo, Norway
Abstract: This paper presents an investigation on payload position and pointing control capability of an hexapod system. It highlights the major mechanical and electrical requirements, and it is useful to guide the detailed design of the system, allowing it to achieve the target pointing accuracy. The SAGE III experiment hosted on the International Space Station is analyzed and the hexapod carrying the payload is designed. The simulation of the dynamic behavior of the system is performed in the most general way, modeling the characteristics of the actual components supposed to be used: actuators driving motors with embedded position sensors, actuators mechanics in presence of thermal disturbances, and reference sensors dynamics. Results presented concerning this mission prove the feasibility of the application: the system meets the target pointing precision and accuracy during all the mission phases, guaranteeing sufficient disturbance rejection capabilities. This result, as well as parametric studies of the system, stresses the savings that can be achieved by adopting the hexapod solution to the pointing and vibration suppression problem.

Title: AMTS: A PROJECT FOR INTERNAL ROBOTIC AUTOMATION
Publication: IAC 1994 congress proceedings, 45th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  9–14 October 1994, Jerusalem, Israel
Abstract:
AMTS (Automated Manipulator Transportation System) is a program, funded by ESTEC and managed by ALENIA SPAZIO as leader of an industrial team, aimed at the implementation of a robotic facility, internal to the ISS European laboratory, to assist astronauts in performing microgravity experiments. A centralized automation concept has been selected.
The system basically consists of a) a manipulator arm, mobile on a 3-axis gantry structure over the overall module volume, able to operate on each individual payload rack and b) a ground control segment, including a planning and programming station for normal, telescience and contingency operations and a simulation and training facility.
The manipulator arm, of anthropomorphic type, is 1.8 m long, has 7 degrees of freedom and is derived from the concept developed by ASI (the Italian Space Agency) for the SPIDER Project, a prototype Engineering Model of which is being subjected to the final integration tests.
The system configuration is described together with the main operational, functional and technological aspects, with a particular emphasis on the microgravity compatibility, for which a dedicated test campaign has been started. Although the detailed design is specific for the COLUMBUS laboratory, the system architecture, due to its inherent characteristics of centralization and modularity, is flexible enough to support a wider range of potential applications in the field of the space microgravity laboratories.

Authors: ['P.G. Bakker', 'T.J. van Baten', 'P.Ph. van den Broek', 'C.B. Guyt', 'B.T.C. Zandbergen']
Title: Delft University Research in space launcher technologies
Publication: IAC 1994 congress proceedings, 45th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  9–14 October 1994, Jerusalem, Israel
Abstract:
In this paper the (Advanced) Space Launcher Research program of the Delft University of Technology, Faculty of Aerospace Engineering, will briefly be described, including some of the major results obtained sofar. The research program was initiated early 1992 and is supported, in part, by the Netherlands Agency for Aerospace Programs (NIVR). The main goal of the research program is to perform (long-term) research necessary to develop advanced technologies for future space launchers and (re)entry capsules and to allow improvement of the Faculty’s curriculum.
The main activities in the program are coordinated with Dutch industry and research institutes as part of a joint research program on advanced technologies for space launchers, referred to as AEOLUS.
The Faculty’s research program includes system analysis, aerothermo-dynamics, flight dynamics, and structures and materials. The investigations concerning systems analysis and flight dynamics concentrate on fully integrated design and design optimization, 6 degrees of freedom flight simulation and joint state- and (aerodynamic) parameter estimation. The studies on aerothermodynamics aim to improve the numerical simulation of (high) super- and hypersonic airflow, including the accompanying heat transfer and chemical reactions. The studies on structures and materials concentrate on high thermally-loaded structures in super- and hypersonic airflows and on the use of fibre-metal laminates.

Title: RISK MANAGEMENT IN THE NORTH SEA OFFSHORE INDUSTRY: HISTORY, STATUS AND CHALLENGES
Publication: IAC 1994 congress proceedings, 45th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  9–14 October 1994, Jerusalem, Israel
Abstract: There have been major changes in the UK and Norwegian offshore safety regimes in the last decade. On the basis of accumulated experience (including some major accidents), there has been a move away from a rigid, prescriptive approach to setting safety standards; it is now recognised that a more flexible, "goal-setting" approach is more suited to achieving cost-effective solutions to offshore safety. In order to adapt to this approach, offshore operators are increasingly using Quantitative Risk Assessment (QRA) techniques as part of their risk management programmes. Structured risk assessment can be used at all stages of a project life-cycle. In the design stages (concept and detailed design), these techniques are valuable tools in ensuring that money is wisely spent on safety-related systems. In the operational stage, QRA can aid the development of procedures. High quality Safety Management Systems (SMSs), covering issues such as training, inspection, and emergency planning, are crucial to maintain "as- designed" levels of safety and reliability. Audits of SMSs should be carried out all through the operational phase to ensure that risky conditions do not accumulate.

Title: THE CARINA SYSTEM: PROJECT STATUS AT THE END OF THE DETAILED DESIGN PHASE
Publication: IAC 1994 congress proceedings, 45th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  9–14 October 1994, Jerusalem, Israel
Abstract:
The CARINA (CApsula di RIentro Non Abitata) Satellite is a system devoted to micro gravity experimentations with re-entry capabilities.
The program is headed by ALENIA Spazio as Prime, under Italian Space Agency (ASI) Contract. The objective is to realise a platform for independent flight opportunities to help scientific and industrial communities in developing space utilisation programs. The design guideline allows, furthermore, to accommodate payloads to perform studies in different disciplines such as Earth Observation and Astronomy. The design has been developed through a low cost approach leading to a very simple and flexible configuration.
In fact, it is composed by two distinct modules: a reentry module that houses the microgravity payload to be returned to Earth and by a service module that supports all the Satellite function during the operative lifetime.
The design of the configuration has been based on the selection of already qualified equipment and units avoiding complexities and the need for heavy control procedures. The present paper illustrates the status of the project at the end of the detailed design B2 Phase, emphasising the features of the Satellite that is now ready to undergo the last development and manufacturing C/D Phase. In particular, it reports of the further technological developments carried out, during the B2 Phase, in the areas that are peculiar of a system that has re-entry capabilities. The description of the foreseen updated mission profile is also given with regard to the nominal mission phases pointing out the specific peculiarities of re-entry, aerodecelerated descent and splashdown events.

Title: CONCURRENT ENGINEERING FOR SPACECRAFT ENVIRONMENTAL TESTING A EUROPEAN SOFTWARE DEVELOPMENT STATUS
Publication: IAC 1993 congress proceedings, 44th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  16–22 October 1993, Graz, Austria
Abstract:
To improve their competitiveness space industries have to improve their reactivity and product quality (performance, realiability, environmental robustness, ...). This leads to the implementation of the concurrent engineering approach as well as a better integration of environmental engineering to the spacecraft design and development process.
In this paper are surveyed relevant technologies to integrate environmental testing and engineering to the spacecraft development process including analysis. Emphasis is given on technical data base technologies and software infrastructures.
A status is presented on a major software development project in Europe called DynaWorks®. Present capabilities of this software are presented. DynaWorks® usage by ESA, European spacecraft prime contractors and test organizations is illustrated by typical examples :
- Spacecraft laboratory test data analysis,
- Hubble Space Telescope (HST) in-orbit data analysis.
Finally, future plans for software development are presented.

Title: Configuration management: Innovation through standardization
Publication: IAC 1993 congress proceedings, 44th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  16–22 October 1993, Graz, Austria
Abstract:
Cooperation in space systems acquisition and development is a consolidated practice in Europe. Aimed to promote the collective technological advancement while uniting the economic resources, naturally induces fragmentation and multiplication of businees arrangements, thus increasing project management costs.
The economical viability of European space projects can be enhanced by promoting integration and uniformity of management practices.
This paper considers the case of Configuration Management (CM), the discipline that coordinates and controls the establishment and evolution of requirements and design data during a system life-cycle, and discusses how an adequate level of standardization and automation of its processes can be reached. First the approach of major space agencies is reviewed and a number of issues identified from a sample of space projects. This will show how a number of fundamental CM elements (e.g., baseline management, Configuration Item selection, CCB responsibilities) simple in principle, can become controversial in their implementation and lead to highly divergent practices.
The paper then suggests, instead of the current project oriented CM practices, an alternative approach based on the application of a two sets of standard requirements. The first set is focused on the organization, and is addressing the standardization of critical CM processes, contractual data formats and terminology. The second set’s target is on project specifics (system complexity, project phase, Integrated Logistics Support (ILS) needs) and provides (additional) tailorable requirements with guidance for application.
The resulting CM system stresses the element of organizational centralization while maintains the minimum amount of project differentiation. It allows for widespread and cost effective automation of CM activities, internally to each organization and at organizational interfaces, while respecting the autonomous choices of the involved organizations.
It is concluded that standardization of CM for European space projects can contribute to lower
project management costs. It can open further advanced opportunities in global automation and digital exchange of data, and as a "catalyzer” for continuous improvements implementation (e.g., Total Quality Management, Concurrent Engineering etc.).

Title: ENVIRONMENTAL EFFECTS ON PASSIVE THERMAL CONTROL MATERIALS OF THE SPACE STATION FREEDOM
Publication: IAC 1993 congress proceedings, 44th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  16–22 October 1993, Graz, Austria
Abstract: The long-life Space Station Freedom (SSF) has power and weight requirements that are not to be exceeded during the detailed design development. There are requirements for both minimum and maximum temperatures associated with allowable fluid temperature ranges as well as prevention of astronaut injury during extravehicular activity, such as frozen or burned skin. In selected areas, temperature gradients must be controlled to prevent distortion of the primary structure. SSF will fly in low Earth orbit, in which atomic oxygen, ultraviolet radiation, meteoroid/orbital debris impacts, and plasma coupling are considered some of the most damaging constituents. These, in conjunction with hardware-induced contamination, required McDonnell Douglas Aerospace to focus on thermal control coatings based on the more durable metals, oxides, and fluorinated polymers. This paper describes the approach and rationale that McDonnell Douglas Aerospace employed for SSF Work Package 2 to provide the required thermal control coatings and insulation to ensure that the operational temperatures remain within acceptable limits.

Title: Overview of the JEM Program
Publication: IAC 1993 congress proceedings, 44th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  16–22 October 1993, Graz, Austria
Abstract:
Japan is Internationa1 will provide Module (JEM)
participating in the Space St.ation Program and the Japanese Experiment which will be attached to the NASA Space Station core system. The phase C/D design and development of JEM was initiated in early 1990. NASDA completed its preliminary design review in 1992 and is currently proceeding with the detailed design of the JEM system and the manufacture of the engineering models of JEM components to be used for system tests. In parallel with this JEM development activity, NASA has been conducting space station redesign from February 1993. NASDA has assessed the redesign impact on the JEM interface. This paper will describe the current JEM design and development activity as well as NASDA's redesign impact assessment.

Title: Space Station Freedom Redesign Status
Publication: IAC 1993 congress proceedings, 44th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  16–22 October 1993, Graz, Austria
Abstract:
This paper discusses the recent redesign activity undertaken by the Space Station Freedom program to determine program options that could meet impending budgetary reductions. The options included both programmatic and redesign variations to baseline Space Station Freedom (SSF). The programmatic options pursued include extending the mission time between assembly flights (gapping), delaying the First Element Launch (FEL), and curtailing or deleting the content of program milestones such as Permanently Manned Capability (PMC).
Redesign options included both alternative configurations and reductions in overall capability such as electrical power and thermal capacity; deferral of Space Station elements such as the airlock, cupola, or habitation module; reduction of subsystem capabilities and redundancies; and simplifications in the detailed design areas.
The technical and programmatic impacts of each option were evaluated and compiled to determine those combinations that could best meet budgetary limitations while retaining maximum capabilities to meet Space Station requirements.

Title: END-TO-END VERIFICATION OF JEM OPERATIONS
Publication: IAC 1992 congress proceedings, 43rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 August–5 September 1992, Washington, United States
Abstract: The Japanese Experiment Module (JEM) will be launched in 1998 and will be utilized and operated at sites in Japan and the US. This paper describes mamly the methods of evaluating and verifying the JEM operability at each mile stone of JEM operations system development. JEM operability will be assessed in the early phase of system design, and the results will be reflected in the development activities in the more detailed design phase. JEM operability will be verified by reviewing the design documents in the early phase of system development. Testing of physical systems will be the major method of the verification in the final portion of the development cycle. In addition to this general approach, an end-to-end verification of JEM operability is planned. JEM Flight Demonstration (JFD) is planned to accomplish this end-to-end verification. The NASA Space Shuttle will be used for this demonstration. In the JFD project, the JEM Remote Manipulator System (JEMRMS) Small Fine Arm (SFA) will be tested by replacing JEM Orbital Replacement Units (ORUs) on the Shuttle Orbiter. This will be carried out by the Shuttle crew with the support of ground personnel. This paper also reports the JFD mission.

Title: Integrated Program Management for the 21st Century - II
Publication: IAC 1992 congress proceedings, 43rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 August–5 September 1992, Washington, United States
Abstract:
Complex aerospace development programs of the 21 st century, such as advanced communication satellites, will require new levels of integration of available system engineering and program management tools and procedures. The changing world environment and the demise of the Cold War is resulting in shrinkage of prime contractors, first tier contractors and lower tier suppliers, and their certified production capabilities. Effective program management in this new environment will require the combination of capabilities embodied in Total Quality Management (TQM), concurrent engineering, integrated product development teams, and risk management.
Existing tools and procedures provide most of what is needed to meet the needs of large, complex programs. Early identification of the likely sources of problems, accurate reporting of status information to the management levels able to act with sufficient authority and resources, and quick execution of corrective actions are the critical ingredients of an effective managementprocess. All of this can be accomplished with careful planning, clear assignment of responsibilities, proper design of reporting procedures and tools, and discipline in the execution of the activities.

Authors: ['M.B. Renton', 'J.M. McKee', 'R.J. Sirko', 'W.H. Siegfried', 'K. Takagi', 'T. Saito', 'S. Matsumoto']
Title: Lunar Base Reference Design
Publication: IAC 1992 congress proceedings, 43rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 August–5 September 1992, Washington, United States
Abstract:
The establishment of a lunar evolutionary base is an important element of several exploration architectures now under review within NASA and other government, industry, and academic organizations. In a project undertaken jointly by engineers at McDonnell Douglas Space Systems Company and Shimizu Corporation, we have developed a conceptual design of a lunar base. We have used the theme of Space Resource Utilization (the Stafford Synthesis Group’s Architecture IV) as a general framework to guide our design. A central feature of our approach is the definition of an evolutionary design that emphasizes resource utilization while proceeding through a series of development phases. We present our overall design, features, and examples of the interactions of various systems and elements with one another. We illustrate how modeling and analyzing these interactions has allowed us to identify performance and cost-benefit analyses,which when completed, will provide data for a more detailed design. We also show how this process has enabled us to review candidate Space Station hardware for a lunar base as well as recommend technology development efforts where necessary.

We have presented a system-level lunar base reference design and evolution strategy. As our design matures, we will gain a better understanding of the detailed evolutionary requirements that will enable transition from First Lunar Outpost to our reference lunar base.

Title: SPACE STATION FREEDOM MOBILE SERVICING SYSTEM - Moving Into the Manufacturing Phase
Publication: IAC 1992 congress proceedings, 43rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 August–5 September 1992, Washington, United States
Abstract:
The Mobile Servicing System, Canada's contribution to Space Station Freedom and a keystone of Canada's space activity, is entering the flight hardware manufacturing phase. The changes resulting from Freedom’s 1990/91 restructuring have been accommodated during the past year, and the detailed design of the first Canadian element to be launched, the Space Station Remote Manipulator System, has been essentially completed. Progress in the detailed design of the other elements is commensurate with their launch schedule.
Preparation for the operations and utilisation phase of Freedom is proceeding, and potential users are being developed by employing a variety of facilities for preparatory experimental work prior to the availability of space station.
Recognition has also been given to the need to enhance technologies, particularly in automation and robotics, to allow the effective replacement and evolution of components of the initial Mobile Servicing System configuration during the thirty year life of space station. Significant progress is being made to this end through an associated, dedicated technology program which seeks to develop the appropriate strategic technologies for the future enhancement of die Canadian contribution. This program is proving to be a useful catalyst for engaging in space activity, small business enterprises networking with the university sector.

Title: THE ESA POLAR PLATFORM: A WORK-HORSE FOR FUTURE EARTH OBSERVATION MISSIONS
Publication: IAC 1992 congress proceedings, 43rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 August–5 September 1992, Washington, United States
Abstract:
In the frame of the European Space Agency (ESA) Long Term Plan, the Earth Observation Missions play a very important role in contributing to a better knowledge and monitoring of the Earth Environment.
Within the range of future Earth Observation missions, the low altitude .Sun Synchronous polar orbit is of special interest because it offers a repeated coverage of the complete surface of the Earth.
For this type of missions, large number of instruments having different technology and application objectives have been developed or are under development in Europe.
To cope with those needs, ESA has initiated the development of the Polar Platform as part of its infrastructure to become the work-horse of future Earth Observation Missions in the Polar orbits.
This spacecraft bus, through its design modularity, can cope with a wide range of payload complements and instrument requirements so that the future development emphasis in Europe can be placed on payload and observations rather than repeated satellite developments.
The Polar Platform design makes maximum use of the SPOT and ERS programmes experience and design in order to reduce development risk and minimise costs. The modular design can cope with different payload accommodation, power and mass requirements as well as different orbit altitudes.
The development is well advanced and definition and is now well into the detailed design and development programme, with components and long lead hardware procurement already initiated. The development of the payload complement for the first mission has been initiated in parallel via the POEM-1 Programme.
The Polar Platform will also make use of the other ESA's future infrastructure, such as the Ariane 5 Launcher as well as the Data Relay Satellite System in order to ensure global coverage of observations.
The launch of the first ESA Polar Platform Mission carrying the POEM-1 Mission is planned for mid-1998.
The performance requirements, design and status of development of the Polar Platform are described in the paper.

Title: Pre-integrated truss assemblies for space station Freedom
Publication: IAC 1991 congress proceedings, 42nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  5–11 October 1991, Montreal, Canada
Abstract:
This paper discusses the recent evolvement of the pre-integrated truss design for Space Station Freedom (SSF). Since 1963 space station concepts have been primarily defined by the era mission requirements, launch vehicle capabilities, and available budgets. The current SSF design activity began in 1983 with the derivation of an ambitious set of mission requirements that resulted in the large truss-based, gravity-gradient-oriented space station. The NASA budget allocation of late 1990 and other factors prompted the most recent program restructuring. As part of this restructure activity, the truss-based concept was reevaluated and retained although the truss itself was reduced in size and changed from a space-erectable design to a pre-integrated design.
The paper summarizes the specifics of the truss evaluation process. Structural models of the truss segments were evaluated in detail and compared in terms of size, weight, construction ease, and cost impact. Specific parameters addressed include the launch weight, surface area and volume for mounting equipment and for maintenance access, assembly techniques, stiffness, deflections, loads, and packaging. It was found that the pre-integrated truss (PIT) would be primarily designed by the loads, stiffness, and deflection criteria imposed by the launch vehicle rather than the on-orbit condition. Of these, the stiffness requirements of each segment mounted in the shuttle payload bay were found to dominate, i.e., to meet a 7 Hz first mode requirement. The evaluation results discussed reveal significant advantages of a pre-integrated truss in the areas of construction ease, reduced extravehicular activity, and construction risk while requiring modest increases in launch weight and redesign cost impact over the space-erectable approach.
The paper then describes the characteristics of the recommended PIT structure design. The main transverse beam of SSF is made up of seven PIT segments that are launched in seven flights after being preassembled on the ground, including complete outfitting of subsystems, utilities, and mechanisms. After the first segment, MB-1, is placed on orbit, a second shuttle launch is berthed to it and the second segment, MB-2, is attached to the former with minimal EVA. This process sequentially continues to complete the transverse beam along with the attached pressurized modules (resource nodes, habitation module, laboratory module, and airlock) to reach a Permanently Manned Capability (PMC) SSF. This results in an overall configuration that maintains the same basic capabilities of the erectable truss concept and the configuration while simplifying the construction technique.
The PIT segments themselves are in two basic lengths (540 and 280 in.) and each consists of aluminum bulkheads, longerons, and diagonals. The overall PIT cross section is hexagonal to provide flat faces for subsystem component mounting and maintenance access, to furnish a corridor for the mobile transporter that traverses the length of the truss on rails, and to supply trunnion mounting locations for installation in the shuttle payload bay. The large cross- sectional beams (up to 3 by 5 in.) are bolted together. Integral utilities are shown routed through the structure to service the surface-mounted subsystem components. An attach mechanism and six bolts provide the mechanism for structurally connecting each PIT segment. Utilities are attached using EVA. Assembly techniques are shown along with a comparison of the attributes of the pre-integrated truss with the prior erectable truss.

Title: The space station Freedom mobile servicing system - The challenge of managing in changing time
Publication: IAC 1991 congress proceedings, 42nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  5–11 October 1991, Montreal, Canada
Abstract:
The Mobile Servicing System, Canada's contribution to Space Station Freedom, is close to completion of its detailed design phase. Circumstantial changes affecting this project in the past year include the integration of Canada's space activities under the umbrella of the new Canadian Space Agency; economic difficulties affecting both Canada and the U.S.; and the major Space Station Freedom Program restructuring exercise undertaken by NASA and its international partners. The Canadian Space Station Program has been adjusted accordingly and it remains as a key element of Canada’s space activity and of Space Station Freedom.

Le Système d'entretien mobile, la contribution du Canada à la Station spatiale Freedom, en est à la phase finale de la conception détaillée. Les circonstances qui ont influencé des changements au projet depuis un an incluent le regroupement des activités spatiales du Canada sous le couvert de l'Agence spatiale canadienne; les difficultés économiques affectant le Canada ainsi que les Etats-Unis; et l'exercice de la restructuration du Programme de la station spatiale Freedom entrepris par la NASA et ses partenaires internationals. Le Programme canadien de la station spatiale a été modifié en conséquence et demeure un élément clé des activités spatiales du Canada et de la Station spatiale Freedom.

Title: Space experiments of Deployable Boom and Umbrella Test satellite (DEBUT)
Publication: IAC 1990 congress proceedings, 41st  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  6–12 October 1990, Dresden, Germany
Abstract: This paper describes the results of the in- orbit performance testing of deployable and retractable umbrelja and boom systems, which will be used as important subsystems of Boomerang/Tether satellites. The umbrella is one of the possible candidates of aerodynamic brake (ADB) system for boomerang satellite and the Boom is also one of the possible candidates of relative position adjusting mechanism between center of mass and aerodynamic force center of the boomerang satellite and initial release/final recovery mechanism of the tethered satellite. For this technology verifications, a small and inexpensive satellite, named DEBUTfDeployable Boom and Umbrella Test Satellite), was developed in a short period of 1.5 years elapsing from the start of the detailed design until the launch of the mission. The lithium dry cell batteries were used as the primary power and functioned normally during 10 days mission lifetime.

Title: Ariane 5 a mature development programme
Publication: IAC 1989 congress proceedings, 40th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–13 October 1989, Malaga, Spain
Abstract:
The Ariane 5 development is
progressing according to plans. Most preliminary design reviews are completed or about to start and detailed design and testing is being performed at sub-system level. Full scale tests of Vulcain motor components have been successful and demonstrate the predicted behaviour. These components will be integrated into a complete motor to be fired in July 1990. Development tests at system level are planned to start in mid-1991. Ground facilities are rapidly taking shape in French Guiana. Much of the civil engineering work will be completed by the end of the year and the facilities will be commissioned in 1991 for system-level tests. Thinking beyond Ariane 5 has already started. Various options are open to increase performance or decrease cost on derivatives of the hardware presently being developed.These derivatives can lead to a whole panoply of vehicle that are technologically well within reach. These vehicles will have to be compared to other, perhaps more "exotic", designs before selecting the successor to Ariane 5.

Title: Development status of Japan's new launch vehicle: H-II rocket
Publication: IAC 1989 congress proceedings, 40th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–13 October 1989, Malaga, Spain
Abstract:
The H-II launch vehicle is being developed by the National Space Development Agency of Japan (NASDA), to meet the demands of Japan's applications satellite users for cost-effective, heavy- lift launches in the 1990s. At present, NASDA is conducting detailed design and development tests in preparation for the first test flight in 1993.
This paper describes the present status of the design and development of the H-II launch vehicle. Special attention is given to the test results of the solid rocket booster and the payload fairing. The updated overall configuration and system descriptions are also presented.

Title: On the status report of the H-II rocket
Publication: IAC 1988 congress proceedings, 39th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  8–15 October 1988, Bangalore, India
Abstract:
The H-II launch vehicle is being developed by the National Space Development Agency of Japan (NASDA), as its main workhorse in the 1990's, to meet the demand for larger satellite launches at a lower cost. At present, NASDA is proceeding the Phase D study (Detailed Design) and many kinds of development test. And manufacturing of Ground Test Vehicle (GTV) and first Flight Model(FM) of H-II will start by this year, towards the first test flight in early 1992.
This paper describes the present status of the design and development of the H-II launch vehicle.

Title: Short-length high-performance cryogenic stage
Publication: IAC 1988 congress proceedings, 39th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  8–15 October 1988, Bangalore, India
Abstract:
A short, high-performance cryogenic upper stage was designed for optimum performance when launched with an attached payload by an NSTS 65K Orbiter. Both high-thrust and low-thrust versions were considered. The goal of the study was to maximize the length and mass of the payload that could be launched in the 60-ft cargo bay. The stage includes a forward liquid hydrogen (LH2) tank and an aft toroidal liquid oxygen (LOX) tank with the main engine located within the toroidal tank void space.
Integrated stage configurations were developed for both high-thrust and low-thrust missions based on detailed design and analysis of the tank, fluid management and thermal control hardware. The effect of 7-day and 30-day loiter times prior to GEO transfer was assessed. A single, common toroidal tank configuration for both thrust levels yielded the lowest vehicle production cost with negligible performance penalty. The resulting stage accommodates payloads up to 38.5 ft in length in the Orbiter and is capable of providing over 17,000 Ibm at GEO. When launched with the current 50 to 55K Orbiter or the Titan IV ELV, the stage is capable of placing over 13,000 Ibm in GEO. These results are discussed and vehicle modifications to provide stage reusability and man-rating are identified.

Title: A matter-antimatter propulsion system for manned interstellar flight
Publication: IAC 1987 congress proceedings, 38th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–17 October 1987, Brighton, United Kingdom
Abstract: The major problems of interstellar flight are addressed in an integrated design of a star ship, Valkyrie. It employs a large diameter (~1 km) thin superconducting current ring to magnetically channel the reaction products from repetitive pellet explosions (either matter- antimatter or fusion) to generate thrust. The thermal intercept fraction on the star ship is very small, ~10-®. Waste heat is radiated to space by a droplet radiator, which also protects against interstellar dust/gas. Maximum velocities in the range 10 to 20% of light speed appear possible.

Title: A get-away special experiment to measure the carbon dioxide content of the earth's atmosphere
Publication: IAC 1986 congress proceedings, 37th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  4–11 October 1986, Innsbruck, Austria
Abstract: This paper describes a Get-Away Special experiment to measure the carbon dioxide content of the earth's atmosphere using the two micron wave-length band of the infrared. A detailed design of the experiment is presented treating both electro-optical and mechanical components. It is also shown how the experiment will be integrated into the Space Shuttle in compliance with NASA regulations. Payload special requirements, interfacing with NASA equipment, thermal design and payload safety are considered. Estimations of the overall mass of the experimental package, power consumption and the amount of data are given.

Title: Japan's new launch vehicles: H-I and H-II
Publication: IAC 1986 congress proceedings, 37th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  4–11 October 1986, Innsbruck, Austria
Abstract:
The development phase of the HM 60 engine, now named VULCAIN, was initiated at the end of 1984 in order to allow the first flight of the ARIANE 5 launcher in mid 1995. Detailed design of the main components of’ the engine (turbopumps, thrust chamber, gas generator) was completed and testing of fullscale components (dynamic seals, bearings) or subscale models (combustion chamber, injector element of gas ’generator) has been started. The first prototypes of the
main chamber, fuel turbopump and gas generator will be manufactured in 1986 and will be tested starting in 1987.

Title: An approach to solar system exploration in the 1990's
Publication: IAC 1982 congress proceedings, 33rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  27 September–2 October 1982, Paris, France
Abstract:
Many exciting challenges exist in the exploration of the solar system. A particularly challenging set of missions for the 1990's has been chosen for investigation by the Mariner Mark II Development Flight Project. These missions include comet and asteroid rendezvous, outer planet flybys (including Titan) with probes and orbiters such as a Saturn orbiter with repeated Titan flybys. The objective of the Mariner Mark II Project is to develop concepts which will permit carrying out such missions at considerably lower cost than past missions of equivalent complexity.
The selected mission set and the associated science objectives and typical science payloads will serve to envelope the requirements for Mariner Mark II in its treatment of the spacecraft and ground system designs and the implementation approaches to achieve the lower costs. The paper will describe, the selected missions and their characteristics along with the science objectives and typical science payloads. The preliminary concepts for reducing mission cost and the overall approach to be taken by the study will be discussed. The first project to be based upon the Mariner Mark II Project results would start in fiscal year 1987 or fiscal year 1988 depending upon the launch opportunity for the selected first mission. The program plan is therefore based on a pre-project effort of a minimum of four years.
This will permit in-depth cost reduction studies and the preparation of detailed design and implementation guidelines for use by Mariner Mark II based projects.

Title: Prediction of thermal expansion coefficients of sandwiches using finite elements methods validated by experimental test results
Publication: IAC 1982 congress proceedings, 33rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  27 September–2 October 1982, Paris, France
Abstract:
The new generation of telecommunication antennas for space applications working at high frequencies, above 20GHz, (wich will be generally martifactu- red by sandwich structures) jneeds an accurate thermostructural design due to the envisaged increase of the dimensions of the reflectors and the related decrease of the required thermal distortion RMS.
In an integrated design which takes into account the reciprocal influence of thermal and structural aspects, the thermal expansion coefficient (C. T.E. ) of the coupled s tructures, which are part of the reflector assembly, is a very important parameter.
A good prediction of this value leads to an accurate estimation of the electrical performances of the antenna system in orbit.
This work describes a prediction method to evaluate the C.T.E. of a sandwich va lidated by some esperimental results and checked by an analytical study. Numerica1 results illustrate the procedures; graphs and appendices complete the work.
KEY WORTS:
antenna, sandwich, skins, adhesive, honeycomb, C.F.R.P. , thermal expansion, RMS, finite elements.

Title: A spaceborne laser range and range rate finder and a potential application for earth oriented research
Publication: IAC 1979 congress proceedings, 30th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  17–22 September 1979, Munich, Germany
Abstract:
Under ESA study contract a conceptual design has been developed for a standard spaceborne laser radar instrumentation. Detailed design activities are the object of ongoing work. The instrument can acquire and track targets in space up to range of 250 kilometers and perform range measurements with a minimum resolution of 10 centimeters improving to 1 centimeter at closer distances (less than 10 kilometers). Range rate measurements are performed with an accuracy of 10 micrometers per second. The paper presents a concise survey of instrument design principles an characteristics and describes an application in geodesy and geophysical research.
Applying the "sate!1ite-to-satel1ite tracking" method in the "low-low" mode, two passive spacecraft, carrying laser reflectors will be tracked by the laser radar installed on a suitable platform. For the purpose of a first mission study the Space Shuttle represented such a platform, and the targets were conceived as sub- satellites to be launched from the Shuttle Orbiter.
It will be shown, that range and range rate measurements performed with the descri bed laser instrument will provide information on the detailed medium wavelength structure of the Earth’s gravity field.

Title: Integrated design of composite materials
Publication: IAC 1966 congress proceedings, 17th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  9–15 October 1966, Madrid, Spain
Abstract:
Three years ago at the XIVth Congress, we presented our first attempt to describe the behavior of composite materials on a rational basis.1 Since then, composite materials have been under intensive research and development as a result of advances in the fabrication of boron and other high- performance filaments and whiskers. The purpose of this talk is to present the state of the art of composite materials as of 1966. Emphasis is placed on the micro and macromechanics analysis from which design methodology of composite materials can be derived.
A very popular application of composite materials is in the form of plates and shells consisting of layers of unidirectional composites. It is a commonly accepted assumption that each constituent layer is quasi-homo- geneous. This assumption leads to the use of the theory of laminated anisotropic plates and shells which has been treated by many authors.2-5 The buckling problem of anisotropic laminated shells have been solved by CHENG and HO,6 and TASI.7 Composite materials offers an opportunity to perform integrated design which combines the traditional structures design with materials design. In addition to the structural analysis of anisotropic laminated plates and shells, micromechanical relations, which links the composite moduli with the properties of the constituent materials, must be known to effect a complete systems integration.

Title: Systems Design - A team effort
Publication: IAC 1965 congress proceedings, 16th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  13–18 October 1965, Athens, Greece
Abstract: To acquaint fourth and fifth year students with the problems and practice of creative engineering of complex systems, the faculty in Aeronautics and Astronautics at Massachusetts Institute of Technology has developed a very successful course in Systems Design. With cooperation from students and faculty from other Departments and from experts from industry and government, the students organize into a team effort with a project leader and subsidiary groups to provide specialized support. With student initiative and enthusiastic faculty support, an integrated design slowly and haltingly takes shape with progress strongly dependent on adequate intercommunication, the identification of key parameters, and responsible and timely effort. The process is illustrated by excerpts from the recent Manned Mission to Mars.

Title: Same title as paper # 1963-31
Publication: IAC 1963 congress proceedings, 14th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  25 September–1 October 1963, Paris, France
Abstract:
This paper presents the detailed design of the attitude control system (ACS) of the Orbiting Geophysical Observatory (OGO).* The OGO is a genera) purpose scientific satellite capable of operating in a wide variety of orbits, and capable of carrying up to fifty different experiments. The orbits can range from 150 naut. mile circular orbits to cislunar orbits.
The attitude control system maintains one body axis of the satellite in alignment with local vertical. In addition, the angular orientation of the satellite body about local vertical is controlled along with a single-degree-of-freedom solar array to maintain the solar cells perpendicular to the Sun’s rays. Further, an orbital plane experimental package (OPEP) free to rotate with respect to the body about local vertical is kept aligned at all times in the orbit plane.
Mission requirements are stated, and from these, control laws for each of the five axes of control are deduced. Response requirements are then stated and the foundation for the control system design is established.
The sensors and control torque sources for the OGO ACS are described and their choice justified. The control system logic is presented, and finally, the details of the system design and sizing are given.

Title: The design of the attitude control system for the orbiting geophysical observatory
Publication: IAC 1963 congress proceedings, 14th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  25 September–1 October 1963, Paris, France
